/.title: Tauira
/.content:
## Tauira — Autoethnographic Knowledge Graph **Tauira** maps the entanglements of a collaborative classroom as a living rhizomatic network. Each node is a participant — Material, Knowledge, or Instinctual — and each edge records a relational force between them across encounters.
> Explore encounters in the sidebar, or open the [Rhizomatic Map]({{< relref "/map" >}}) to navigate by term.

/artefacts/.title: Artefacts
/artefacts/.content: Teaching artefacts — lesson plans and classroom documents referenced across encounters.

/artefacts/artefact-001.title: Artefact 001 — Collaborative Writing Lesson Plan (T1 W3–W4)
/artefacts/artefact-001.content:
## Learning Intentions

- Students will draft a 400-word collaborative argument using the Assessment Rubric criteria.
- Students will practise peer-editing using the four-criteria feedback protocol.
- Students will identify one aspect of the rubric that they find constraining and one they find enabling.

## Materials

- Assessment Rubric (NCEA Level 2 collaborative writing, laminated, one per student)
- Whiteboard markers (four colours)
- Draft response booklets (one per group of four)
- Timer visible to students

## Lesson Plan

| Time | Activity | Notes |
|------|----------|-------|
| 0–5 min | Silent reading of the rubric | Students annotate: circle one criterion they understand, underline one they find unclear |
| 5–10 min | Table discussion: share annotations | Each group nominates a scribe; tables are arranged in cluster near the whiteboard |
| 10–25 min | Collaborative draft — 400 words | Whole group works toward shared argument; rubric on desk for reference |
| 25–35 min | Gallery walk: read another group's draft | Two representatives stay at table, two rotate |
| 35–45 min | Peer-edit using rubric criteria | Focus on one strength and one suggestion per criterion |
| 45–50 min | Reflection: which criterion helped most? | Open discussion; teacher notes responses on whiteboard |

## Assessment

This lesson plan is an anonymised teaching artefact. Student names do not appear in any column. Group identifiers (Table A, Table B, etc.) are used in the original record.

The rubric referenced here is the NCEA Level 2 collaborative writing rubric, distributed in W2. It appears in the node graph as **node-003 (Assessment Rubric)** and is active across both [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] and the W4 encounter.

## Notes

- Round tables (node-001) supported the cluster seating arrangement essential to this task.
- Boredom (node-005) was observable in the first ten minutes; the gallery walk partially addressed this.
- This lesson plan was not followed exactly in W3 — the S3 joke event interrupted the sequence at the 10-minute mark.

/encounters/.title: Encounters
/encounters/.content: Classroom encounter records — primary data units of the Tauira autoethnographic knowledge graph.

/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W3-L2.title: W3-L2 — The Deadline on the Desk
/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W3-L2.content:
This encounter opened with low affective energy. The assessment rubric, distributed the previous week, seemed to weigh on the room. Boredom was visible in the first fifteen minutes — bodies angled away from the board, minimal eye contact with the task.

The turn came when S3, seated at the cluster of round tables near the window, held up their laminated rubric and remarked, deadpan: *"This looks like something you'd find at a funeral."* The laughter that followed was collective and immediate. See [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] for the recurrence of this affective pattern.

The assemblage of round tables, laminated deadline, and S3's comedic interruption formed what I am calling the *table-deadline-joke cluster* — a repeating configuration across T1 that shaped the affective texture of writing lessons. For analytic reflection see [[memo-001]].

/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W4-L1.title: W4-L1 — What If Knowledge Had No Centre?
/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W4-L1.content:
Three students were absent. Their absence structured this lesson as much as those present — the room felt different, thinner. The [[Assessment Rubric]] from W3 was still on several desks, a material residue of the previous week's constraint.

The introduction of [[Rhizomatic Thinking]] through Deleuze and Guattari produced a slow, cautious engagement. I moved table-by-table, asking each group their entry point. The rearranged tables — less clearly oriented toward any centre — afforded this differently from the standard arc configuration.

This was the first lesson I explicitly theorised the table arrangement. See [[memo-002]] for gap analysis and [[essay-001]] for the theoretical synthesis across all three encounters.

/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W5-L3.title: W5-L3 — S3 Hands the Rhizome Back
/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W5-L3.content:
S3 arrived before the bell. I watched them rearrange a chair near the window and then, after a moment, replace it exactly as it was. This small act of anticipatory arrangement stayed with me throughout the lesson.

The blank whiteboard held the room in a different way from the previous two encounters. No instruction, no deadline — just space. When I asked what students remembered from W4, S3 spoke immediately: *"Everything connects to everything and nothing connects to anything."* The room laughed. See [[essay-001]] for the theoretical reading of this moment.

The *theory-laughter bridge* — the connection between [[Rhizomatic Thinking]] and collective affect — crystallised in this encounter. For the accepted gap suggestion identifying the blank whiteboard as an unnamed material participant, see [[memo-003]].

/essays/.title: Essays
/essays/.content: Autoethnographic essays — theoretical accounts synthesising encounter data across the term.

/essays/essay-001.title: On the Table-Deadline-Joke Cluster: An Autoethnographic Account
/essays/essay-001.content:
## Introduction

Three lessons. Three round tables. One recurring joke. This essay asks what the repetition means — not as a management problem or a pedagogical opportunity, but as a structural feature of the classroom encounter itself.

I draw on Karen Barad's (2007) agential realism to argue that the assemblage I call the *table-deadline-joke cluster* was not produced by any single agent but emerged from the intra-action of material arrangement (the round tables), knowledge artefact (the assessment rubric), affective presence (S3's humour), and instinctual response (laughter, boredom). I also draw on Deleuze and Guattari (1987) to read the classroom's knowledge structure as rhizomatic — multi-entry, decentred, lateral.

---

## Encounter One: The Deadline as Uninvited Guest (W3-L2)

In [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]], the assessment rubric arrived on each desk before the students did. Laminated. Yellow. The room's energy was flat — what I am calling *boredom* in the node graph. S3 named the rubric as a funeral document and the room laughed.

What Barad helps me see here is that this was not S3 acting on passive students. The joke was an intra-action: S3's body, the rubric's material authority, the sound of the mower outside, the round table configuration that placed certain students at the edge of the room's attention — all of these co-produced the event. The laughter was not caused; it was assembled.

Deleuze and Guattari's rhizome is also present here: S3's joke entered the lesson from a lateral direction, bypassing the planned learning sequence and producing a different knowledge-entry entirely. The rubric, intended as a hierarchical guide to correct writing, was momentarily deterritorialised.

---

## Encounter Two: The Absent Students (W4-L1)

In [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]], three students were absent. Their absence structured the lesson as a trace — in Derrida's sense, a presence-through-absence. I moved differently through the room. I spoke more carefully. The *rubric-table-theory triangle* assembled here: the previous week's rubric still lying on some desks, the rearranged tables, and the introduction of Deleuzian rhizomatic thinking as the lesson's content.

The whiteboard question — *What if knowledge had no centre?* — named the theoretical stakes explicitly for the first time. Students engaged cautiously. The low ambient energy of the room, the absent chairs, the question hanging in the air: these intra-acted to produce a lesson that felt unresolved even as it ended.

### The Rhizome as Pedagogy

Introducing rhizomatic thinking while the tables were arranged without a clear front produced what I want to call a *performative contradiction* in the best sense: the form enacted the content. Multiple entry points. No obvious centre. The students who arrived without the prior week's context could enter anyway, from wherever they were.

---

## Encounter Three: S3 Hands the Rhizome Back (W5-L3)

In [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]], the blank whiteboard waited. S3 arrived early and rearranged a chair, then replaced it. In that gesture — the preparation and the withdrawal — I read something of what Barad means by anticipatory intra-action: S3 shaping the space before the lesson's official beginning.

When S3 rephrased the rhizome as *"everything connects to everything and nothing connects to anything"*, the room laughed. But this was different laughter from W3. It was not the laughter of relief from the rubric's authority. It was recognition — the sound of a room finding itself in a concept it had been living with for two weeks.

The *theory-laughter bridge* assembled here: node-004 (Rhizomatic Thinking) and node-006 (Laughter) in their closest conjunction. See [[memo-003]] for the accepted gap suggestion that the blank whiteboard deserves its own node.

---

## Conclusion

The table-deadline-joke cluster is not a metaphor. It is a naming of an assemblage that structured three lessons, produced affective shifts I could not predict, and put pressure on my understanding of what teaching is. Barad asks us to take material participants seriously as co-producers of knowledge events. Deleuze and Guattari ask us to abandon the root-tree model of knowledge in favour of the rhizome. Both framings illuminate something the cluster makes visible: that my experience as a teacher-researcher is constituted *with* participants, not *for* them.

---

**References**

Barad, K. (2007). *Meeting the universe halfway: Quantum physics and the entanglement of matter and meaning*. Duke University Press.

Deleuze, G., & Guattari, F. (1987). *A thousand plateaus: Capitalism and schizophrenia* (B. Massumi, Trans.). University of Minnesota Press.

/memos/.title: Memos
/memos/.content: Analytic memos — reflective writing responding to each classroom encounter.

/memos/memo-001.title: Memo 001 — The Groundskeeper and the Threshold
/memos/memo-001.content:
This memo responds to [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]], the first encounter in which the *table-deadline-joke cluster* became legible as an assemblage.

## Gap: The Groundskeeper

The scene description notes the sound of mowing outside the window. I accepted the gap suggestion that this non-human participant — the groundskeeper, the mower, the sound — mediated the room's attention threshold before S3's joke. It produced a low-frequency auditory presence that the classroom was already navigating. S3's joke cut across that texture. The assemblage analysis should name this participant.

## Diffractive Reading 1 — Barad

Read through Barad's (2007) agential realism, the laughter event loses its agent (S3) and becomes an intra-action: the body, the sound, the rubric's authority, and the spatial arrangement of round tables all co-constituted the event. No single element caused the laughter.

## Diffractive Reading 2 — Massumi

The 8-second pause between the laughter and my next utterance becomes, via Massumi, a productive interval — not a failure to manage but a moment in which affect circulated freely. The pause was pedagogical even if unintentional.

/memos/memo-002.title: Memo 002 — Absence as Participant
/memos/memo-002.content:
This memo responds to [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]], the lesson in which three absent students became structuring presences.

## Gap: Naming Absence

I did not accept the gap suggestion in its strongest form — I am not yet ready to commit to "absence" as a named node in the graph. But I cannot dismiss it. The three students who were missing shaped the lesson's tempo, its emotional undertow, and my movement through the room. I avoided the spaces their chairs occupied. I spoke louder than usual, as if to fill.

## Diffractive Reading 1 — Derrida

The absent students left a trace. In Derrida's sense, the trace is not nothing — it is the mark of a presence that was expected and did not arrive. The lesson plan carried the assumption of their presence throughout; their absence produced a perpetual deferral.

## Diffractive Reading 2 — Posthumanist Pedagogy

Snaza et al. (2014) argue that humanist pedagogy is constituted around the present, counted body. My notebook notation of the absent students' names at the end of class was a humanist gesture: an attempt to restore them to presence through inscription.

/memos/memo-003.title: Memo 003 — The Blank Whiteboard as Node
/memos/memo-003.content:
This memo responds to [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]], the lesson in which the blank whiteboard structured the opening in ways I had not fully anticipated.

## Gap: The Blank Whiteboard (Accepted)

I accept this gap suggestion. The blank whiteboard is a Material participant that has not appeared as a node in the graph. Its deliberate emptiness — a choice I made before students arrived — produced a different kind of opening. The room could not orient toward instruction because there was none to orient toward. This created a condition in which S3's joke became structurally necessary, filling the gap that the blank board had opened.

Adding node-007 (Blank Whiteboard) with a `mediates` edge to Boredom (node-005) and Laughter (node-006) would make the rhizomatic map more accurate for this encounter.

## Diffractive Reading 1 — Barad

The blank whiteboard was not passive. It participated. Its emptiness intra-acted with student bodies — those who looked at it expectantly, those who looked away, those (like S3) who read it as an invitation.

## Diffractive Reading 2 — Rancière

The withheld instruction redistributed what Rancière calls the *partage du sensible* — the distribution of the sensible. Students became producers rather than receivers. S3's joke was not disruption; it was emancipated spectatorship finding its form.
